Could you explain this for the...stupid? Does this mean if the file is 100MB you download 100MB and not 110MB? Checksum to me relates to encryption authentication but you have to have the numbers to check against.

A checksum (like sha256sum or md5sum) generates a hash, usually from the contents of a file. If the file is of a different size than the original, it would normally result in a different hash. Collisions (two different files with same hash) are possible, but only sha1sum is known to be vulnerable to collisions as in someone can create a sha1sum colliding file in a reasonable amount of time. Otherwise the other checksum methods are secure in that making a collision would take far too long and it is very unlikely for two different files to have the same hash by chance. In short, the uniqueness of a hash is a guarantee that the file you download is actually the right file and not some other file (such as malware).

EDIT: A checksum uses every byte of a file as input to generate the hash. So if one byte differs, the hash will usually be different.

I also note that, if all you want to check is transit damage, sha1 is still perfectly valid, as the odds of creating a colliding file by chance are still astronomical. It just isn't valid to check for maliciously altered files.

Not exactly, but checking the file size isn't a bad basic precaution. Basically a checksum is a cryptographic hash, that easily allows a file to be verified as authentic. Basically what it does is use a formula to condense the file down to a random string of 20 or 30 letters and numbers. If the file is changed at all, even slightly, this number will be completely different. So generally a software developer would include this reference hash with the file download, so you can calculate the hash of the file yourself and check to see if the download matches. If the hash is different, then the file is likely compromised.
